verdict.reasoning: Patient reports wheeze starting about two days ago and associated shortness of breath: "it started, like, about two days ago" and later "I'm feeling like a little bit, uh, uh, short of breath."

Patient links onset to dust from house-cleaning and timing about an hour later: "I was, like, cleaning the house. And, like, um, all this dust came out of the, the carpet" and when asked if wheeze started suddenly, replies "it started after maybe, uh, an hour or so."
Patient states dyspnea interferes with completing sentences: "when I'm, you know, talking, um, to my friends, I start finding that, uh, sometimes, um, I'm unable to , complete my sentences."
Patient denies chest pain and dizziness: to pain with deep breath, "Mmm, no, no. No pain." and to dizziness, "Uh, no. No dizziness. Uh, none of that."

Doctor asks about eating and drinking and patient reports several glasses of water daily: "have you been eating and drinking OK, particularly water?" and patient: "Yeah, yeah. I think I'm having, like, you know, four or five glasses a day."

Transcript: "I used to have, like, a bit of, um, asthma, uh, as a child" and currently with exertional symptoms: "sometimes when I, um, run for, like, long periods, it can, it can start up a bit. But, um, I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler. I use that." This reflects ongoing asthma with exertion, not just childhood asthma that is only "occasionally" treated; the fact understates current asthma status.
Patient reports seasonal hay fever: "also in the summer I sometimes get, um, hay fever."

Patient has an inhaler but not currently in active/regular use and details are not specified: "I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler. I use that" and later "I think I might have one from, like, a couple of months ago." No further details are given.
When asked about medications for hay fever, patient replies: "Not really," indicating no regular antihistamine use.

Patient suspects dust sensitivity but does NOT deny known drug allergies specifically; the doctor only asks "apart from this, do you know if you're allergic to anything?" and patient answers "not that I know of." Drug allergies are never mentioned, so claiming denial of known drug allergies is additional and specific beyond the transcript.

Doctor indicates concern for asthma or allergy as cause: "given you've got a history of asthma and hay fever. This could be one of two things. But, we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first." This supports that wheeze and shortness of breath are thought likely due to asthma flare or allergy-related bronchospasm.

Doctor advises taking an antihistamine on the way to the surgery: "if you've got something, like an antihistamine... I would take one" and "You might be able to get one on your way to the doctor's surgery. If not, they can prescribe you one." This corresponds to over‑the‑counter antihistamine advice en route to GP.

Doctor mentions pulse-ox but not lung exam or peak flow explicitly: "use a small device on your finger, to check the amount of oxygen in your blood." No same‑day specification, lung exam, or peak flow is stated in the transcript.

There is no instruction to bring the existing inhaler, no explicit mention of SABA, and no directive for GP to consider oral steroids; only general statement: "you may need to take some steroids now. But, we... won't be able to know until we've done those tests first."
Doctor states: "I'm gonna write a letter for your GP" and later "You should get the letter over the app. And then, we can, you can take yourself to the GP."
The transcript contains no discussion of red‑flag symptoms or instructions to seek urgent/emergency care if symptoms worsen.
